title: UX in 2027 may be less about interfaces and more about behavior
text:
UX in 2027 may be less about interfaces and more about behavior

The signals I see today point to more adaptive interfaces, more delegated actions, and a larger responsibility for designers to define the limits

The most important change in UX may not be visible on a screen.

Software is beginning to interpret goals, assemble interfaces, choose tools, and act on a person’s behalf. Google Search can now generate interactive graphs, simulations, and mini apps in response to a query. Google’s A2UI project lets agents compose interfaces from trusted component catalogs. Gartner expects task-specific agents to appear in 40% of enterprise applications by the end of 2026.

None of those signals proves what UX will look like in 2027. Together, however, they point to a shift in the object we design. A fixed flow describes what a person can do. An adaptive system must also define what the product can infer, generate, and do for that person.

My own use of AI is much less dramatic than the demos. I use it to organize information, recover details from transcripts, prepare placeholder copy, name layers, connect variables, and explore product data. In a financial organization, confidentiality and internal policy sharply limit where experimentation is appropriate. That gap between public capability and responsible use is not incidental. It is part of the design problem.

This is not a prediction that interfaces will disappear. It is an evidence-based hypothesis: if software takes on more decisions and actions, UX will need to spend more of its craft defining behavior, limits, and ways to return control.

The interface is not disappearing, but it may stop telling the whole story

Traditional software waits for a sequence of instructions. Agentic software is designed to interpret a goal, plan steps, use tools, and return with a result.

That changes what an interface needs to do. I can make this concrete with two ERP products I worked on earlier in my career. AppHealth had to be modernized and standardized across an ecosystem that included financial and management operations. AzulControle also concentrated operational rules, records, and reports in a conventional ERP structure.

Consider one recurring management task: understanding why the financial result for a period changed. In a fixed ERP, the manager first chooses a company or unit, selects a date range, opens a financial report, applies categories and status filters, compares the result with another period, and often exports the data to assemble an explanation elsewhere. Each step may be valid, but the system asks the person to translate a business question into its information architecture.

An intent-based version could begin with: “Why did this unit’s result fall compared with last month?” The system could identify the relevant period and unit, compare revenue and expense categories, surface the largest variations, and compose a chart for that question.

The interface would not end there. Before the analysis could support a decision, it would need to show which records were included, which definition of “result” it used, whether any data was missing, and how the comparison was calculated. If the manager asks the system to act, such as changing a forecast or approving a payment, permissions, confirmation, and a reversible record become mandatory.

This example changes the flow from navigation by system structure to navigation by intent. It does not eliminate the ERP’s complexity. It relocates some of that complexity into interpretation, where mistakes can be harder to notice.

These figures show how quickly companies are experimenting with agentic AI. They also make cost, business value, and risk controls increasingly important when deciding where greater autonomy is actually useful.

From fixed flows to constrained adaptation

Generative UI is often described as an interface created or adapted according to a person’s goal and context. Nielsen Norman Group connects the idea to outcome-oriented design, in which the experience focuses more directly on the user’s desired result.

We already see small versions of this when an AI conversation produces buttons, checkboxes, tables, or other controls instead of asking the user to type everything. The important part is not that AI can generate a button. It is that the system is beginning to choose which interaction makes sense at that moment.

Google is already testing a more literal version of this idea. Its 2026 Search announcements describe generative interfaces that build custom graphs, trackers, dashboards, simulations, and mini apps for a query. Google Research reported that people strongly preferred its generative UI prototypes to baseline language-model responses, while interfaces built by experts still received the highest ratings. The signal is meaningful, but so is the limitation: generation improved the response without replacing design expertise.

By 2027, more interfaces may behave like temporary explanations of what the system understood, what it recommends, and what it still needs from the user.

I do not think this will make fixed interfaces obsolete. Stable structures support learning, spatial memory, predictability, and confidence. These qualities matter even more in healthcare, finance, government, and enterprise products, where a vague status or misunderstood permission can affect an entire operation.

The useful direction, in my view, is not unlimited personalization. It is constrained adaptation. The system can respond to context, but inside boundaries defined by accessibility, business rules, permissions, consistency, and risk.

This is also why UX cannot become a recipe executed by an agent. What works for one audience, product, or operational context may fail in another. The difficult part is noticing those differences.

When software starts acting, trust becomes part of the interaction

There is enough movement around agents to take them seriously. Gartner projected that up to 40% of enterprise applications would include task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, compared with less than 5% in 2025.

The counter-signal is equally important. Gartner also forecast that more than 40% of agentic AI projects may be canceled by the end of 2027, citing cost, unclear business value, and inadequate risk controls.

These figures show how quickly companies are experimenting with agentic AI. They also make cost, business value, and risk controls increasingly important when deciding where greater autonomy is actually useful.

What Brazil reveals about agentic AI adoption

Brazil provides a useful example of how uneven AI adoption can affect the development of agentic products.

Cetic.br reported that AI use among Brazilian companies grew from 13% in 2024 to 17% in 2025. The difference by company size was substantial: 50% of large firms used AI, compared with 15% of small firms. Across OECD countries with available data, 52% of large firms used AI in 2025, compared with 17.4% of small firms.

Trust, then, may become a set of interaction primitives: permission, provenance, confirmation, receipt, reversibility, and escalationThe gap matters for UX because an interface can be identical while the conditions behind it are not. One company may have clean data, specialized teams, cloud infrastructure, and mature governance. Another may depend on fragmented records, manual processes, outsourced technology, and little capacity to monitor an agent after launch.

In that second environment, token consumption is not an abstract technical detail. It affects which interactions are economically sustainable. A generated analysis may look effortless while requiring repeated model calls, retrieval, validation, and infrastructure that the organization cannot support at scale. A system that depends on perfect data may also fail precisely where automation appears most attractive.

Brazil is therefore useful to a global discussion, not as an exception but as an intensified version of a common problem. The OECD describes an emerging AI divide in which larger firms, knowledge-intensive sectors, and more innovative regions move faster. Designing for 2027 means designing across that unevenness, including lower-cost fallbacks, explicit uncertainty, human escalation, and experiences that still work when the agent cannot.

For designers, trust can no longer mean only explaining a recommendation. If a system can act, people need to understand what it will do, which information it can access, when it will ask for confirmation, and how an action can be interrupted or reversed.

McKinsey’s analysis of the automation curve in agentic commerce makes a useful distinction: delegation is likely to vary according to trust, regret risk, and the value of human involvement. Reordering a familiar product is different from choosing an investment, approving a financial operation, or making a healthcare decision.

Regulation is moving in the same direction. Since August 2026, the European Union’s AI Act transparency rules have required people to be informed in certain situations when they are interacting with AI. The European Commission’s Article 50 guidance also addresses machine-readable marking of generated or manipulated content.

Trust, then, may become a set of interaction primitives: permission, provenance, confirmation, receipt, reversibility, and escalation.

Products may need to work for people and their agents

Another signal changes the meaning of the word user. Nielsen Norman Group describes AI agents as users, interacting with products alongside people. Google’s Universal Commerce Protocol offers a concrete example of infrastructure designed to let AI surfaces communicate with merchants and perform actions such as checkout.

The customer remains human, but a machine may search, compare, interpret, and operate the product before the person sees the final result.

This makes structured content, APIs, permissions, error handling, and machine-readable policies part of experience design. A person may never reach a product if their agent cannot understand its information, verify a rule, or complete a task safely.

It also creates a new risk. Optimizing only for agents could flatten brands and experiences into whatever is easiest for a machine to compare. Designing only for humans could make the product invisible or unusable in delegated journeys. UX may need to mediate both without forgetting who ultimately lives with the consequence.

Research can become faster without becoming automatically better

My own experiments with website data show both sides of AI-assisted analysis. Connecting analytics and Search Console data can help me identify patterns, profile the real audience of the site, understand how people arrive, and find opportunities for new content. It can bring signals together much faster than reading isolated reports.

But a generated persona is not automatically a real person, and a correlation is not an explanation. The output is useful when it helps me ask better questions. It becomes dangerous when a polished synthesis makes assumptions look like evidence.

Maze’s Future of User Research Report 2026 found that 69% of researchers were already using AI in their workflows. Respondents still considered interpreting nuance and emotion, making ethical decisions, and framing the right questions areas where human involvement was essential.

This matches what I see in practice. AI can help recover information from a call, group data, summarize patterns, and suggest hypotheses. The designer or researcher still needs to know what was lost in the summary, whether the sample supports the claim, and whether the finding makes sense in that specific context.

Research may therefore become faster at processing and more demanding at judgment. We will also need to research the AI itself, testing how it behaves across ambiguous requests, incomplete context, conflicting constraints, and failures. A successful happy path tells us very little about a probabilistic system.

Design systems are becoming context for machines

I am already seeing the beginning of this discussion in design systems. Teams are exploring Figma and FigJam automation, component generation, and ways to document a system so that an AI agent or MCP integration can understand components, variables, layers, naming, and usage rules.

This is close to what I have started testing with Figma’s AI. Layer naming or variable linking can save time, but only when the tool understands enough of the local structure. Without context, automation creates another cleanup task.

Figma’s 2026 AI Report, based on 8,403 survey responses and 639 qualitative interviews, found that the boundaries between design and development were already becoming more porous. The share of designers participating in development doubled to 41%, while developers doing design work increased from 44% to 60%.

If agents generate interfaces and code, design system documentation must explain more than what a component looks like. It needs to express when the component should be used, what it can contain, how states behave, which accessibility rules are mandatory, and which alternatives should be avoided.

Google’s A2UI project makes this direction tangible. Instead of allowing an agent to send arbitrary executable interface code, A2UI lets it describe an interface using components from a catalog controlled by the receiving product. The agent can compose an experience, but the client retains control over rendering, styling, security, and available components.

Components become vocabulary. Tokens become constraints. Documentation becomes context. Governance becomes a way to prevent plausible output from drifting away from the product.

Does the designer become an auditor?

There is an uncomfortable consequence to this shift. If machines generate more screens and states, designers may spend more time reviewing outputs, writing constraints, checking exceptions, and investigating failures. The craft can begin to resemble system auditing.

Some of that work is necessary. A probabilistic system cannot be evaluated only through a polished happy path. Someone needs to test ambiguous requests, conflicting permissions, incomplete data, accessibility failures, and actions that cannot easily be reversed. The object of critique expands from a screen to a range of possible behavior.

But turning designers into quality control for machine output would be a poor future for the profession. It would place UX at the end of the process again, approving what a model or engineering system has already produced. It would also confuse governance with design.

The more useful role begins earlier. Designers can help decide which intentions the system should support, which decisions it may make, what evidence it must expose, what remains stable, and when it must stop and ask a person. Writing agent-readable rules is part of that role, but so are research, framing, prototyping, and the creation of new interaction models.

The day-to-day craft may therefore split into two connected activities. One is generative: imagining the relationship between a person and a system that can interpret and act. The other is evaluative: testing whether that relationship remains understandable, inclusive, and accountable across many possible outputs.

This is more than prompt writing. A prompt describes a desired response. Product constraints define an operating space. They connect research, policy, data, components, permissions, business rules, and recovery. If designers only polish prompts, the role narrows. If they shape that operating space, the role becomes more consequential.

Accessibility cannot be a final check in a generative system

The WebAIM Million 2026 detected more than 56 million accessibility errors across one million home pages, an average of 56.1 per page. At the same time, the average number of elements on those pages grew 22.5% in one year, reaching 1,437.

That relationship between complexity and errors should make us cautious. If AI can generate new states, layouts, controls, and content, accessibility cannot depend on someone reviewing a few predefined screens at the end.

It must exist inside the components, constraints, generation rules, automated tests, human evaluation, and monitoring. Accessibility itself is not a trend. What may change is how impossible it becomes to treat it as a static checklist.

What the evidence suggests for 2027

The signals do not support a world without interfaces. They support interfaces that are more adaptive, conversational, and connected to systems capable of acting.

They also show a gap between enthusiasm and maturity. Agent adoption is accelerating while projects are being canceled for cost, weak value, and inadequate controls. Generative interfaces are becoming more capable while expert-designed experiences still outperform them. AI speeds up design and research work while human judgment remains essential for nuance, ethics, and framing.

Taken together, these are not separate contradictions. They describe the work ahead.

Figma’s State of the Designer 2026 found that 89% of 906 surveyed designers said AI helped them work faster, 80% said it improved collaboration, and 91% said the tools improved their designs. The same report presents craft as a human differentiator.

Faster execution does not reduce the need for judgment. It increases the number of possible outputs that someone must evaluate.

If a system can create alternatives, UX still needs to decide which problem deserves attention. If it can adapt an interface, UX needs to define what cannot change. If it can act, UX needs to establish permissions, recovery, and accountability. If it can summarize research, UX needs to decide whether the evidence supports the conclusion.

By 2027, the role of UX may include drawing fewer predetermined paths and defining more of the boundaries within which a system can create a path. That is still a hypothesis, not a certainty. But it is one that current products, research, standards, and adoption data now make possible to test.

The interface will remain important. It just may no longer be the whole experience.

References and further reading

  • Figma, State of the Designer 2026. Research conducted with 906 digital designers across multiple regions about AI adoption, speed, collaboration, craft, and the changing role of designers.
  • Google Research, Generative UI: A rich, custom, visual interactive user experience for any prompt. An experimental comparison of generated interactive experiences, baseline language-model responses, and expert-designed sites.
  • Google, Search I/O 2026 updates. Product examples of Search generating graphs, trackers, dashboards, simulations, and mini apps in response to queries.
  • Google, Introducing A2UI. An open project that allows agents to compose interfaces from component catalogs controlled by the receiving application.
  • Figma, 2026 AI Report. A three-year study based on 8,403 survey responses and 639 qualitative interviews with designers, developers, and product managers.
  • Maze, The Future of User Research Report 2026. Research about the adoption of AI in user research and the areas in which human judgment remains essential.
  • Nielsen Norman Group, Generative UI and Outcome-Oriented Design. An analysis of interfaces that can adapt or generate elements according to the user’s context and desired outcome.
  • Nielsen Norman Group, AI Agents as Users. A discussion about products being accessed by AI agents alongside human users and what this changes for UX and accessibility.
  • Gartner, 40% of enterprise applications will feature task-specific AI agents by 2026. A forecast about the rapid integration of task-specific agents into enterprise software.
  • Gartner, Over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027. A counterpoint to accelerated adoption, highlighting cost, unclear value, and inadequate risk controls.
  • Cetic.br, AI use by Brazilian companies reached 17%. Results from the TIC Empresas 2025 survey of 4,174 companies, including adoption differences by company size.
  • OECD, AI use by individuals and firms in 2025. Official cross-country data showing the adoption gap between large and small firms.
  • OECD, Emerging divides in the transition to artificial intelligence. Analysis of uneven AI adoption across firm sizes, sectors, and regions.
  • McKinsey, The automation curve in agentic commerce. An analysis of how trust, regret risk, and the value of human involvement can determine the appropriate level of delegation.
  • European Commission, Guidelines on transparency obligations under Article 50 of the AI Act. Official guidance about informing people when they interact with AI and marking generated or manipulated content.
  • Google, Universal Commerce Protocol. Technical documentation for an open standard that allows AI surfaces to interact with merchants and perform commerce actions.
  • WebAIM, The WebAIM Million 2026. An accessibility analysis of one million home pages, including detectable errors and changes in page complexity.

title: Neuroqueering design practice
text:
Neuroqueering design practice

A look into design as a craft through the lens of neuroqueering.

I remember reading Robert Chapman’s Empire of Normality at a strange threshold: in my mid-twenties, a few years into design as a profession, still in a pandemic haze, and on the precipice of what felt like great change. I was discovering a world where fellow neurodivergent thinkers and authors pushed boundaries, revealing a space of possibility beyond the dominant narratives.

That rather prolonged period of personal discovery later coincided with a rapid shift in my role toward design leadership. I found myself seeking guidance not solely as a craft expert, but as a not-so-experienced mentor and coach. Fresh into this new reality, I felt a lot of insecurity in my own aptitude to be the design leader I wanted to be, and still need to be. That insecurity manifested itself both as an internal force and as a response to the general state of anxiety amongst designers of the mid-2020s. I still think about this piece by Sara Wachter-Boettcher every day.

At times, it was hard for me to connect this personal state of being (a queer, autistic person just trying to figure it out) with my work as a new design leader (a manager and coach really trying to figure it out). But recently, I’ve found even more reinforcement and inspiration in the critical work exploring neurodiversity and queerness. Such work reaffirms and reshapes how we think of our bodyminds, and has plenty to offer to our design practice too.

In Neuroqueer Heresies, Dr. Nick Walker introduces “neuroqueering” as a practice of subverting, disrupting, or defying the neuronormative and heteronormative structures. With its roots in Queer Theory, the concept explores how these power structures reinforce each other, and how we may find collective liberation through engaging in interconnected practices that challenge them. The definition is broad, but Dr. Walker sees neuroqueering as an action first.

That underlying idea of subversion and transformation is one that I recognise in design itself. To me, design, with its many shapes, has always been just that: a transformative and mediating force between people, technology, and futures.

The greatest joy I’ve found in my work recently came from close partnership with fellow design professionals. It’s also come from truly seeing just how much of a changing force design can be, as an inherently explorative discipline which looks forward in time. The paths towards the futures diverge, and there’s nothing more challenging and rewarding than trying to make sense of it as a collective, for the collective.

The routes into design can diverge greatly, too. People come from traditional and non-traditional educational backgrounds, shift trades, and learn on their own. Regardless, we share something in common: we want to create and solve something, to make our days as humans lighter or more enriching.

Returning to Dr. Walker’s framing of neuroqueering as an action, I wondered if there was a way for me to translate this philosophy into practice that we can employ as designers. To me, the underlying themes are about challenging essentialism, conventional form, and determinism.

To flourish, we must challenge normalcy and binary thinking. In other words, it means rejecting the idea that there’s a boundary within which our craft must correspond to what the dominant power systems consider the appropriate way to craft a design or experience a design. The neurodiversity paradigm is in direct opposition to the pathology paradigm: the former sees variations of brain function and behaviour as a natural part of human diversity, while the latter perceives neurodivergence as a disorder.

Chapman explores this further in Empire of Normality, tracing how the pathology paradigm intertwines with the illusion of normalcy as a scientific, economic, or social truth, a myth that has perpetuated great harm (including but not limited to the popularisation of eugenics and white supremacist rhetoric), especially for marginalised communities.

We see the language of marginalisation deeply entrenched in design practice. Consider the term “edge case”, a concept describing a supposedly unlikely scenario of how a person uses a design. When actively employed in craft, such thinking can reinforce our biases and assumptions to varying degrees of exclusion, regardless of intent.

In Design for Real Life, Eric Meyer and Sara Wachter-Boettcher reframe “edge cases” as “stress cases”. This shifts the burden away from people experiencing the design towards responsible and considerate action on the part of designers. “Stress case” as a concept communicates urgency, as it highlights how a design may not correspond to the context in which it’s meant to exist.

“Dark patterns” is still a widely used metaphoric expression for deceptive, extractive, or simply difficult design patterns — despite it aligning with harmful, anti-Black sentiments which draw parallels between “darkness” and “maliciousness”. Lately, designers have been reaching for “deceptive patterns” as a natural descriptor for such phenomena, which also communicates the concept much more clearly without covering it in metaphor.

Language, of course, shapes how we understand our craft, but design as a discipline can also be bound by conventional form. We can understand conventionality as patterns and principles firmly rooted in our understanding of design, be that in its interaction, or in visual presentation. Such forms may be informed by the actions of dominant players in the field, groupthink, or simply trends that seek to benefit the few rather than the craft itself.

Determinism, in both what and how we craft, is the antithesis of design. Take for instance the push of AI as an unavoidable technology, one that will embed itself in every facet of our craft. It’s a discourse dominated by the urgency of a conviction: get on board now, or be left behind.

We’ve seen it before. Technology changes. Because design is a mediating force, its core is about building a deeper understanding and connection between our craft and the world it inhabits. Such determinism forces us to teach each other the wrong lesson: that our craft’s worth amounts to speed over reflection, or tool prowess over judgement and intentionality.

This year, my team and I have worked on formulating what great design means to us. Although we’ve been working together for months, years in some cases, we hadn’t really stopped, together, to build consensus around what great design actually is. Our conversations were revealing: alongside human-centricity, reflection, and delight, we kept returning to systems-thinking as the thread that ties great design together.

Each principle plays its own part in our philosophy. Systems-thinking specifically raises an interesting duality: convention can be both a guideline and a signal for change. Systems change. We want to abstract and extend the conventions that work, but remain alert to the parts of a system that create barriers or mismatches in experience. That’s where we complement systems-thinking with design that centres people, that is in dialogue with its context, and that seeks moments of lightness and joy.

To me, this is what neuroqueering design practice is: the radical idea that there is no normalcy, that how we do design and what we design are subject to exploration and subversion, to design for people, for dignity, and for purpose.

Kristina (she/they) is a design leader based in Finland. Kristina writes about inclusive design, being autistic at work, and thinking in systems.

title: The Best Perfumes Of 2026, According To Our Fragrance-Obsessed Editors
text:
The Best Perfumes Of 2026, According To Our Fragrance-Obsessed Editors

In a beauty editor’s world, being forced to declare a favorite beauty category is like choosing a favorite child — you simply can’t expect us to pick. But we make no apologies for admitting that fragrance holds a very special place in our lives (and our routines).

A compliment on your perfume can be incredibly affirming, but there’s something even more poignant about fragrance’s ability to transform how you feel when you wear it purely for yourself. For us, fragrance is a constant: at the office, at the gym (controversially), and, yes, even at home when no one else can smell you. With that in mind, we take our fragrance very seriously here at Refinery29. Over the past few years, we’ve made it our mission to sniff out, test, wear, and discuss the latest launches alongside the classics — so we can recommend the ones that are truly worth your time, money, and shelf space.

That’s why we wanted to give the very best of them their moment in the spotlight with our Fragrance Awards 2026. From niche, under-the-radar houses to the biggest names in perfume, these are the 29 scents we’ve spent the past few years smelling, spritzing, and talking about with our friends and colleagues.

Who knows? You might even discover your new signature.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Best New Fragrance: Byredo Future Memories Eau de Parfum, $235 for 50ml

“Mark my words: Future Memories is going to become the fragrance Byredo is best known for, even usurping cult classics like Bal D’Afrique and Gypsy Water. At first spritz, it’s a generous pour of vanilla-steeped whiskey, but the intoxicating boozy notes soon unfold into tobacco-like iris butter, cozy orange blossom, and salty, skin-like musk. If a 1920s speakeasy were a fragrance — all cigar smoke, strong cocktails, and perfumed lapels — it would be this, despite the “future” in its name. And the staying power! I sprayed it on a jacket over a month ago, and it’s still as hypnotic as it was on the first day.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Luxury Fragrance: Penhaligon’s Halfeti Eau de Parfum, $330 for 3.4 fl oz.

“I would say the enduring popularity of Halfeti needs to be studied, but the reason is obvious: Nothing smells as expensive and seductive on my skin as this does. Even ten years after its launch, I have a hard time comparing it to anything else. Warm, cozy saffron, cardamom, and nutmeg jump out at first, but over time, creamy sandalwood, cocooning amber, and comforting musks come into their own, making it nuzzly and inviting. I love wearing it on my neck and wrists, and whenever I pull someone in for a hug, they never fail to compliment me. In fact, anything from Penhaligon’s is the epitome of luxury to me, but Halfeti trumps them all.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Drugstore Fragrance: Le Monde Gourmand Tomate Bébé, $30 for 30ml

“Le Monde Gourmand is known for its vast array of affordable eaux de parfums, and this past spring it added Tomate Bébé to its roster. The fragrance, made in collaboration with iconic Los Angeles restaurant Jon & Vinny’s, is everything an aspiring tomato girl wants to smell like. As the name suggests, it’s a vegetable-forward blend of green pepper, tomato leaf, and fresh basil, but with citrusy lemon verbena, skin-like ambrox, and a whisper of dessert-like caramel. The result? A perfume that’s good enough to eat — almost.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer

Best Niche Fragrance: Ex Nihilo Demon Dancer, $180 for 50ml

“Ex Nihilo is one of those brands perfume enthusiasts talk about in hushed tones, as if keeping it to themselves will help them gatekeep it — it’s that good. I’ve tried pretty much every scent from the niche perfume house and found favorites in Blue Talisman and Fleur Narcotique (the latter said to be adored by Hailey Bieber), but I think the latest addition to the brand’s burgeoning fragrance dynasty blows them all out of the water. Tart rhubarb, zippy peppermint, and sharp, green blackcurrant give it such an intriguing edge that you can’t help but smell yourself — the notes practically dance off the skin — while vanilla-esque tonka and warm musks ground it, making it the perfect everyday scent.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Designer Fragrance: Miu Miu Miutine Eau de Parfum, $108 for 30ml

“Strawberry scents had a big year (see: The 7 Virtues Strawberry Jam and Phlur’s Strawberry Letter), but I’d argue that no fragrance has captured the fruity note quite like Miu Miu’s Miutine — the house’s first new scent in six years. With notes of juicy strawberry, heady gardenia, warm brown sugar, and cozy vanilla, it’s everything the Miu Miu woman is: playful, feminine, and a little offbeat in the best way. And can we have a moment for the bottle, please? Inspired by Miu Miu’s iconic matelassé leather goods, it’s every bit as chic as the juice inside.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer

Best Celebrity Fragrance: Billie Eilish Your Turn II Eau de Parfum, $70 for 30ml

“Billie Eilish: Grammy-winning recording artist, Gen Z style icon, and…the front-runner in the celebrity fragrance game. One of her more recent drops, Your Turn II, is a darker, woodier interpretation of the original fresh-fruity scent. (In a 2025 interview, the singer actually revealed that Your Turn II was an earlier fragrance sample she’d loved but hadn’t ever seen the light of day.) I personally love the blend of more feminine perfumery with accords more commonly used in colognes. Case in point: jammy fig and cassis clashing with zesty vetiver and resinous olibanum. (Not to mention, the lasting power of this rivals some of my most pricey perfumes.) Safe to say, with it emerging as a fan-favorite, she made the right call rescuing it from the vault.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer

Best Genderless Fragrance: Lore Somewhere but Nowhere Eau de Parfum, $92 for 50ml

“I rarely ambush my husband with fragrances, but I’ll never forget the first time I sampled Lore’s Somewhere but Nowhere — and immediately knew I had to smell it on him. It cites Americana as its north star, but to me, it smells like home (or your person — more or less the same thing, really.) Its heart of cedarwood mixed with creamy cardamom and black tea (and a barely-noticeable touch of whipped vanilla cream) makes this one that I love as much on him as I do on me. Which means one thing: We’re going to need a larger bottle.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer

Best Everyday Fragrance: Merit Retrospect L’Extrait, $92 for 30ml

“Merit had no business going this hard with its fragrance debut, but hey, we’re certainly not complaining. The inaugural scent, Retrospect, is exactly what you’d expect from the makeup brand that mastered minimalism: Effortless yet impactful, and with a certain mysterious quality. No one note really stands out; you just smell really good. However, we can reveal the notes in the warm, sheer scent: Bright notes of citrusy bergamot and fresh pear meet a floral bouquet of jasmine, rose, and violet. The secret sauce, in my opinion, is in the base of warm vanilla, skin-like musk, and leafy moss, giving it a familiar finish. And because it’s an extrait (a more concentrated form of fragrance), you can expect this one to last all day long wherever you apply it.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer

Best Long-Lasting Fragrance: Diptyque Orphéon Eau de Parfum, $260 for 2.5 fl oz.

“During a closet clear-out recently, I pulled out a coat I hadn’t worn in over a year, and the scent that greeted me was unmistakable: Diptyque Orphéon. It’s the perfect paradox. Juniper berries give it a strong gin-and-tonic edge — a tall glass tumbler loaded with ice — while cedarwood, jasmine, and tonka bean evoke a church foggy with incense. The dry down is so special: powdery and comforting, like a blush compact from the ’90s. It’s the one perfume all my beauty editor peers agree on, and the staying power is truly second to none.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Compliment-Earner: Glossier You Doux Eau de Parfum, $82 for 50ml

“Glossier You Doux has earned me so many compliments; it was a front-runner for my wedding-day scent. (I ended up wearing it at my rehearsal dinner.) It’s easily the most wearable, romantic take on a woody fragrance I’ve tried, and like all of the Glossier You scents, it has a musky ambrox base that truly works on everyone. Along with toasted palo santo, it features delicate violet, spicy frankincense, and smoky myrrh. The result is an effortlessly alluring scent with truly unparalleled mass appeal.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer 

Best Travel Fragrance: Dior J’adior Solid Perfume L’Or de J’adore, $109

“We’ve all seen Charlize Theron exiting a pool of liquid gold (or more recently, Rihanna sauntering through Versailles), but Dior’s solid perfume iteration, L’Or de J’adore, somehow makes the iconic scent feel more luxe than ever. Housed in a tiny gold compact that’s basically begging to double as a bag charm, this travel-friendly solid makes it easier than ever to bring your scent on vacay — without fearing it being confiscated by airport security. With notes of heady jasmine, sweet rose, and elegant violet wrapped in a warm, nectar-like finish, I think it’s bold, iconic, and unforgettable.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer 

Best Office-Friendly Fragrance: D.S. & Durga I Don’t Know What Eau de Parfum, $225 for 1.7 fl oz.

“There’s a fine line between wanting to smell good at work and causing perfume cloud-induced headaches from two cubicles away. Here’s where D.S. & Durga’s I Don’t Know What comes in. It’s subtle but noticeable, with a clean, woody, skin-like quality that somehow smells like you — only better. The formula is built around a mix of bright bergamot, iso e super (a synthetic fragrance molecule with moody, amber-like notes), herbaceous vetiver, and musky ambroxan, creating an airy, balanced scent that lingers all day long on skin and clothes without alerting Brenda from HR. In other words, it’s office-appropriate without being boring, and transitions seamlessly to after-hours.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer 

Best Wedding Fragrance: Commodity Milk Orchid Expressive Eau de Parfum by @Perfumerism, $115 for 50ml

“Commodity’s Milk Orchid was one of the most anticipated perfume launches of 2025, but the formerly limited-edition fragrance recently became a permanent fixture in the brand’s collection. Content creator Emma B, aka Perfumerism, collaborated with Commodity to create a gourmand floral that feels elevated yet universally appealing. Creamy notes of fig and coconut milk swirl with orchid to create the perfect light-yet-impactful scent for your big day. This is truly special-event and signature-scent worthy!” — Sophia Dennis, head of programming and brand strategy for Refinery29 & Beautycon

Best Date-Night Fragrance: NOYZ Only Human Eau de Parfum, $85 for 1.69 fl oz.

“Some fragrances can’t help but take center stage. By contrast, NOYZ Only Human is more about making people lean in closer in a “What perfume are you wearing?” kind of way. Which is exactly why it’s taking home our award for best date-night scent. Warm, woody, and subtly sweet, it blends creamy cardamom, comforting sandalwood, dessert-like vanilla, and sultry musk into a skin-like scent that feels intimate yet totally effortless. It’s the kind of fragrance that smells even better up close. Conveniently, right where you want it for date night.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer. 

Best Skin Scent: Cyklar Flora Veil Roll-On Perfume Oil, $24

“If you find traditional floral scents annoyingly loud, you have to try Cyklar’s Flora Veil. It bypasses the heady, garden-in-full-bloom intensity entirely, redefining what a floral profile can be. When I first took a whiff of it, I instantly thought it smelled like me fresh out of the shower, but even better. It earns top honors in the skin scent department because of how masterfully it wears throughout the day. It starts with a delicate (not overly fruity) whisper of crisp raspberry that has just enough brightness to intrigue you without feeling sweet, and it melts seamlessly into a grounding, velvety musk base. Rather than sitting heavily on top of your skin or taking over a room, the oil formula literally warms up with your natural body chemistry, creating your own little bubble of a delightful-smelling aura. What makes Flora Veil so addictive — and why I grab it the most — is the I’m-not-trying-too-hard confidence it gives.” — Alexis Bennett Parker, Refinery29 director of shopping partnerships 

Best Hair Fragrance: Initio Atomic Rose Hair Perfume, $105 for 50ml

“I first smelled this hair perfume on a friend as I leaned in for a hug, and I couldn’t stop thinking about it. I had to buy one for myself, and now I reach for it more than my eau de parfums. Most hair perfumes apply with a whisper and disappear in the breeze, but this clings to strands like an extrait. Lush Bulgarian rose and powdery Turkish rose are heady and mesmerizing, while zingy bergamot cuts through with a hit of freshness. But it’s the vanilla that really sticks around — you’ll find yourself wanting to smell your hair throughout the day. Perhaps an odd habit, but one I can’t kick when I wear this.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Body Mist: Being Frenshe Matcha Me Hair, Body, & Linen Mist, $16.99 for 5 fl oz.

“Body mists are having a major comeback, and when I got a sneak peek (whiff?) of Being Frenshe’s new Matcha Me scent in the Hamptons this summer, I knew I’d found a new favorite. (I’ve been keeping the lab sample in my purse for mid-day touch-ups, and am glad to no longer keep it a secret.) It’s fresh, soft, and uplifting — just like your favorite matcha latte. Alongside the namesake tea note, there’s a hint of soothing vanilla (a favorite of founder Ashley Tisdale French, who also includes it in Vanilla Cashmere) and a soft musk that gives it a cozy, clean quality without veering sugary. Even better, it’s formulated to softly scent everything from your skin and hair to your linens and room for the ultimate relaxing mood.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer 

Best Scented Body Wash: LOoPHA Oud + Amber Hand + Body Wash, $24.50 for 400ml

“Life’s too short not to make every shower a great-smelling one. LOoPHA (aka The Ordinary’s sister body care brand) has arguably mastered the art of the body wash, elevating the humble shower gel with its liquid and powdered body cleansers, which come in three scents: Oud + Amber, Chalk, and my personal favorite, Broadleaf Forest. There’s not a bad one in the bunch, but I can’t get enough of how crisp and clean (not medicinal) Broadleaf Forest smells. It’s cozy, grounding, and makes every shower feel like a moment of calm.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer

Best Scented Body Moisturizer: Brunel Pearl Glow Body Oil, $53

“Capturing that signature, sun-kissed Jasmine Tookes glow has been pinned to the top of my beauty mood board for years. Actually achieving it? Pure chaos. Traditional body oils often turn into a slippery mess, ruining fine silk and making crisp white linen an absolute no-go. But Brunel’s Pearl Glow is the holy-grail pivot. Pearl Glow smells effortlessly high-end. It opens with a bright burst of crisp red apple and warm solar notes that instantly transport you to a golden-hour beach day. As it settles into skin, it unfolds into a lush heart of jasmine petals and creamy almond, before drying down to a grounding, velvety sandalwood base that gives it a bespoke luxury perfume feel. What makes it an absolute award winner, though, is how seamlessly it balances top-tier perfumery with real-life practicality. You get that enviable, lit-from-within sheen without feeling heavy or sticky. Best of all, its dry-touch finish absorbs quickly with zero transfer onto white clothing, meaning you can finally bathe your collarbones in supermodel radiance and walk out the door completely stain-free.” — Alexis Bennett Parker, Refinery29 director of shopping partnerships 

Future Classic Fragrance: Parfums de Marly Delina Exclusif, $265 for 1 fl oz.

“Some fragrances have their moment before fading away; others feel destined to have one for years to come. Parfums de Marly’s Delina Exclusif falls firmly into the latter camp, earning our Future Classic award for its unapologetically luxurious take on the iconic fruity-floral Delina. A richer, moodier sibling to the original scent, it layers juicy lychee and crisp pear with Turkish rose, spicy incense, warm vanilla, and woody oud for a multifaceted, versatile scent that’s sweet but not saccharine. It’s the kind of perfume that instantly feels iconic — and I, for one, wouldn’t be surprised if, years from now, we’re still talking about it.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer 

Best Alcohol-Free Fragrance: Maison Francis Kurkdjian Kurky Eau Parfumée, $195 for 2.4 fl oz.

“Maison Francis Kurkdjian is known for fragrances that smell expensive and sophisticated (hello, Baccarat Rouge 540), but the luxury perfumer is far from a one-trick pony; Kurky Eau Parfumée is a literal and metaphorical breath of fresh air, thanks to its bright, fruity profile. It opens with juicy raspberry and peach mixed with soft florals, light-as-air musk, and creamy sandalwood. And unlike the vast majority of my perfume collection, this formulation is alcohol-free. (“Eau parfumée” literally translates to “scented water.”) As such, it feels less drying on skin than a traditional alcohol-based fragrance, and I also love using it as a hair mist to add scent and a hint of shine. The result is playful yet elevated, proving that an alcohol-free fragrance can have just as much personality as a traditional eau de parfum.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer

Best Fall Fragrance: Phlur Vanilla Canyon Eau de Parfum, $99

“To me, most vanilla perfumes are usually way too sweet, aggressively artificial, or smell like a walking dessert table, which is an instant pass. But Phlur Vanilla Canyon completely flips the script, taking the usually cloying note to grown-and-sexy territory. If you’re already obsessed with Vanilla Skin, consider this its darker, cooler, big sister. It has a smoky vanilla DNA that doesn’t read as buttercream. Think smoldering amber and intoxicating depth that feels grounded. What elevates Vanilla Canyon to true award status is how easily it grabs attention without ever feeling overpowering or suffocating. It gives you that warm, sultry vibe that stays close to the skin, kind of like a plush cashmere sweater, making people instantly lean in to ask what you’re wearing. It takes a note we all thought we knew and reinvents it into a masterclass in modern, mysterious perfumery.” — Alexis Bennett Parker, Refinery29 director of shopping partnerships 

Best Fresh Fragrance: Frédéric Malle Par Acne Studios Eau de Parfum, $295 for 50ml

“Fresh perfumes have somewhat faded into the background, both literally and figuratively, as deeper, heavier gourmands have come to dominate the fragrance conversation — and they’re not exactly known for their staying power, either. But Frédéric Malle Par Acne Studios refuses to be overlooked. It opens with a slightly soapy, aldehydic laundry note, but as it dries down, the magic happens. One whiff and you’re whisked away somewhere that feels as pure and weightless as a fluffy cloud, while still being sharp, crisp, and refreshing.” — Sophia Dennis, head of programming and brand strategy for Refinery29 & Beautycon

Best Gourmand Fragrance: Brown Girl Jane Chalet, $102

“Gourmand fragrances are built around edible, dessert-like notes, and Brown Girl Jane’s Chalet is like stepping into a high-end patisserie in Paris. Think white chocolate truffle offset by slightly bitter dark cocoa, plus ripe, syrupy plum and a dash of vanilla essence for good measure. But I think that the effervescent champagne note cuts through all that richness, making it surprisingly wearable rather than tooth-achingly sweet. It’s one of my most complimented perfumes.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Woody Fragrance: Maya Njie Nordic Cedar, $156 for 50ml

“I first came across Maya Njie’s Nordic Cedar in 2018, and it has been a linchpin in my perfume rotation ever since. If you like Phlur’s Father Figure, you’ll absolutely adore this. Crisp, green cedar and grassy patchouli are warmed up with a dash of cardamom spice and amber, while musk helps it melt into the skin, becoming an extension of you — like the natural scent of freshly washed skin after a long bubble bath. The bottle may be simple, but the juice inside is anything but. It’s layered and intriguing, equal parts fresh and sexy.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Floral Fragrance: Gucci Flora Gorgeous Orchid, $188 for 3.3 fl oz.

“Gucci Flora Gorgeous Orchid was the first floral perfume that I, a longtime floral perfume hater, genuinely loved. And if you suspect that florals simply aren’t for you, allow me to introduce you to the exception. Gucci Flora Gorgeous Orchid takes the traditional, occasionally stuffy perfume category and gives it a modern, gourmand-leaning twist, blending pâtisserie-like vanilla with airy ozonic notes (synthetic accords designed to evoke the atmosphere after a rainstorm) and a subtle vanilla orchid accord. It’s proof that a floral fragrance doesn’t have to smell like a flower shop — and that even a floral perfume skeptic can find their match.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer

Best Green Fragrance: Prada Infusion de Rhubarbe Eau de Parfum, $190 for 3.4 fl oz.

“If you like nothing more than a stroll through the farmers’ market on the weekend, Infusion de Rhubarbe will be right up your alley. Think tangy, crunchy stalks of rhubarb — green leaves and all — freshly pulled from the ground, still earthy and warm. Zingy bergamot, verdant green mandarin, and bitter orange oil add to its bucolic quality, balancing the rose note so perfectly that even those who think they dislike floral scents (me!) will fall head over heels for this. I love the fresh, airy cloud that follows me when I spritz it through my hair.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Oud Fragrance: Kayali Oudgasm Milky Musk Oud Eau de Parfum, $140 for 50ml

“Kayali’s entire Oudgasm collection is a total compliment magnet, but if you ask me, the most special and memorable scent of them all is Milky Musk Oud. It’s like a second skin, or pulling on your favorite cashmere sweater after a long soak in the tub. It’s all down to earthy suede, indulgent whipped cream, soapy white musk, and creamy sandalwood, with strawberry and, of course, oud — a fragrant, honeyed tree resin — adding a peppy sweetness. Unlike other oud scents, oud is the supporting actor rather than the star of the show, but it still has plenty of depth without being overpowering. I can guarantee people will ask what you’re wearing.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Fruity Fragrance: Ellis Brooklyn Plum Tonic Eau de Parfum, $115 for 50ml

“Forget banana, strawberry, or coconut for a hot minute. The fruity note I’m reaching for this fall is purple plum. There’s something rich and brooding about it in all its ripe, syrupy glory, making it feel like a grown-up alternative to the saccharine — and, to be honest, a little juvenile — fruity fragrances out there right now. Plum Tonic is the antidote. It’s still sprightly and energetic thanks to sweet mandarin, while cool, cucumber-like violet leaf, acidulous acai, and warm, enveloping amber crystals give it the rich, complex depth I look for in a fruity fragrance.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director

title: “We Have Not Been Forgotten”: Meet The Palestinian Designer Behind Olivia Rodrigo’s Dress
text:
“We Have Not Been Forgotten”: Meet The Palestinian Designer Behind Olivia Rodrigo’s Dress

Olivia Rodrigo may only be 23, but the pop star knows exactly who she is. The young singer has been vocal about supporting women’s rights since she was a teenager, and recently held the inaugural Daisy Chain Fields music festival — inspired by Sarah McLachlan’s Lilith Fair — raising $20 million USD for women’s charities. During a press conference for the festival, where she announced an initial $10 USD million donation, Rodrigo made waves by stepping out in a Palestinian-designed dress by Nöl Collective. At a time when Palestine is suffering under Israeli occupation, wearing a garment made on the ground with symbols of freedom on it was a strong statement.

“It helped say, ‘We are still here; we have not been forgotten’,” designer and founder Yasmeen Mjalli tells Refinery29. “It meant the world to us.” Mjalli isn’t sure how Rodrigo or her team discovered their fashion brand, but says they were honoured to be chosen, and stayed in contact with her team throughout the process. While the singer’s team suggested some general ideas for the silhouette that aligned with her classic style and the colour pink, Nöl Collective were given more free rein than one might imagine. “We had a lot of creative freedom in the details, such as the shade of pink — a soft and dusty rose — the type of material we use[d], raw silk, [and] details like the flutter sleeves, frilled neckline, the embroidery motifs and the embroidery colours,” the designer explains. “It was so much fun to be given the creative freedom to bring something to life that honoured Olivia’s style while also reflecting our own identity.”

The symbols on the dress are also more than just decoration. While the garment is beautiful, Nöl Collective knows the power that Palestinian embroidery can hold; representing a political reality, the natural world, and our dreams. The design house chose specific motifs to tie into Rodrigo’s ethos and what she stands for. “The flowers spoke to the theme of the Daisy Chain Fields festival. Flowers are incredibly important in our world; they decorate the land after rains, [provide] beauty after a storm, [support] ecosystems, [feed] wildlife, and sometimes [contain] medicinal properties,” Mjalli says. “In this particular instance, the daisy chain symbolizes the power of a united world in the face of adversity.” The dusty rose dress also featured embroidered birds, a clear representation of freedom — not just for Palestinians, but for all those who need it around the world.

Nöl Collective’s garments are handmade in Jerusalem, Gaza, Ramallah, and Bethlehem, and the fashion brand places a strong emphasis on showcasing the entire process. Mjalli knows fashion is inherently political, regardless of where a garment is made. “70% of garment workers in the world are women; it’s a women’s rights issue,” she says. “[And] because fashion has unfathomably detrimental effects on the environment, it’s also an environmental issue.” Fast fashion has been widely criticized for human rights violations and environmental impact, but it’s so easy for consumers to compartmentalize or ignore these issues.

“When you show how the garment is made, you humanize the process and close the gap that separates the consumer from the creator. The hope is that people are more mindful when buying because they can see how much time, labor and love go into a garment,” the designer explains. “We hope that for every garment we put out in the world, you can picture the hands of the women who made them — the same hands which brush hair, pick fruit, and hold children and grandchildren.”

It’s impossible to talk about Nöl Collective without acknowledging the impact the Israeli occupation has had on them. For Mjalli, it’s incredibly hard to put into words how difficult the process of creating garments has been. Moving between cities and towns now takes much longer due to military checkpoints, shipping orders is challenging due to border closures, and customs can destroy shipments at their discretion.

The fashion house uses natural fibres that it is unable to source locally, so it relies on shipments from overseas. Last week, a large shipment of naturally dyed and hand-woven wools from Indian artisans was rejected. “[It was] destroyed last week, simply because of who we are. This was devastating, because our production had already been delayed for months, meaning the collection would be released much later than needed,” the founder says. “We still had to pay the cost of shipping and for the fabric itself because the artisans still need to be paid for their labor, and then we still needed to buy replacement fabric.” The fashion house ended up having to start a GoFundMe to cover the excess costs because fashion and art matter, and it’s a form of resistance to keep going.

Mjalli wants people to understand how vital it is to support Palestinian businesses, especially those on the ground. “We are creating under impossible circumstances,” she says. “Every day, a door slams shut in our face, and we keep searching until we find another door to keep going. So many talented artisans here don’t get a chance, so supporting artisanal work on the ground here can profoundly impact the community.”

title: Lady London’s Bars, Beauty & Brains
text:
Lady London’s Bars, Beauty & Brains

Before she became Lady London, Zaire Stewart was a fly toddler exploring New York City’s unique beauty culture. At just three years old, she was being carted to Dominican hair salons, getting her hair washed and pressed by the same women she still visits today. Her mother kept her dapper in DKNY and Moschino as they traveled between the Bronx and New Jersey. Greatly influenced by the beauty and brilliance of the women in her family, an aunt with an interest in global politics and anti-apartheid messaging recommended her name; it’s no wonder Lady London is such a cultural force. In 2018, Lady London developed an interest in music, built on a foundational love of literature from childhood to college. Lady London joined Naked Beauty to talk about how she discovered she had presence and how she wielded it into a nearly decade-long career and fanbase of more than a million people.

During the conversation, they talked about how she learned to maintain her composure as a public figure and how her confidence can’t be shaken by industry execs or online trolls. Lady London shares that her confidence was well earned, as it took her some time to accept that she could be beautiful and smart without downplaying one or the other. She shares some tips on how to model that self-assurance during the Show & Tell portion of the show, when Lady London demonstrates how not to be baited. Of course, we learn all about her beauty rituals, tips, and favorite perfumes. We got other advice from Lady London, including how she mentors women coming into the industry behind her, and what she’s learned from the hip-hop legend pouring into her. Lady London is a creative force, poet, rapper, executive producer, mentor, and hobby enthusiast. As we learn in this interview, with Lady London, there is always more than meets the eye.

title: The Napoleon Jacket Is Making A Comeback This Fall—Here’s How To Style It & Our Favorites To Shop
text:
The Napoleon Jacket Is Making A Comeback This Fall—Here’s How To Style It & Our Favorites To Shop

Throwing on a bold layering piece is, often, all it takes to make a good outfit great and the timely resurgence of the Napoleon jacket — complete with epaulettes and columns of oversized buttons — among popular trends for 2026 just confirms it.

Despite the summer season still underway, I can’t help but notice the faint chill in the air when the sun goes down, which means colder weather is right around the corner and it’s time to start thinking about fall and winter wardrobes. If you’re like me, and prefer to keep your daily uniform easy yet elevated (think, some iteration of denim and a plain tee), then introducing something a little more festive into the mix as the temperature drops can make all the difference, especially when you want a little more flair. 

Of course, the military jacket is nothing new and has been through its fair share of trend cycles, coming out on the other end more powerful than before. Named after 19th-century French military leader Napoleon Bonaparte, the cropped uniform silhouette has since been adopted by the style set, with Yves Saint Laurent leading the way in the late 1960s. By the ’90s, Jean Paul Gaultier and Thierry Mugler were among some of the big names to put their own spin on the look.

Cultural icons like Michael Jackson and supermodel Kate Moss also began to embrace the trend, with the former making it an integral part of his stage presence. This only further cemented the jacket’s status within the fashion industry. Today, it’s defined by a strongly defined shoulder, navy, gold, white, and red color combos, and, of course, round embossed buttons (functional or not). 



Aside from the likes of Alexander McQueen and Ann Demeulemeester, who have been designing Napoleon jackets for decades, the last few seasons have seen a noticeable influx of brands, big and small, who are influenced by military uniforms. According to fashion psychologist Shakaila Forbes-Bell, this is always a sign of the times, as well as the industry’s current obsession with the indie sleaze aesthetic. “People like to use their style as a way to reflect the current cultural zeitgeist,” she previously told Refinery29. “[Shoppers are] dressing in styles that are a bit more utilitarian and pragmatic.” 

Back in February, I sat front row as Cinq à Sept debuted a fitted denim Napoleon jacket, paired with a pussy-bow blouse on its Fall 2026 runway in NYC. While later in the season, R13 offered a super wearable take on the trend in longline and oversized silhouettes emblazoned with the same large, round buttons you’d expect on more traditional styles. Meanwhile, cool-girl brand EB Denim’s “Ford” Jacket feels like a more posh, updated version that has the same versatility as a classic black blazer. 

DashDividers_1_500x100

How To Style The Napoleon Jacket

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Shelby Ying Hyde (@theshelbyying)

When it comes to embracing the look IRL, the key is to keep it super simple and straightforward, slipping it over generally unfussy ensembles to let the military-inspired details do all of the talking. I paired the vintage, Ralph Lauren version that I found on Poshmark with dark-wash flared jeans and a Tabi ballet flat for a family dinner, like it was 2006. 

Dua Lipa tends to take a more casual approach, wearing bright red and navy cropped styles by Ann Demeulemeester with denim and white T-shirts. Blackpink’s Jennie wore a custom Napoleon jacket by the brand for Lollapalooza in August, opting for a leather triangle bikini top underneath. Whereas, Brother Vellies creative director and founder of the 15 Percent Pledge, Aurora James took a more playful approach, styling her navy blue Napoleon-inspired Chanel Spring 2009 jacket with bloomer pants and mules—before ultimately slipping it over the classic white tee and denim combo, to show the secondhand style’s range. 

Whether you opt for an affordable Napoleon jacket for everyday wear or are looking to invest in a luxury piece for your personal archive, there are a bunch of different styles available on the market to choose from, many of which will make even the simplest of ensembles that much more interesting. The endless styling options are just the icing on the proverbial cake.

Anthropologie’s Beauty Advent Calendars Always Sell Out—And They’re Already Here

It may not feel like it just yet, but there are some telltale signs that fall, let alone the holidays, are indeed right around the corner. It’s not just pumpkin spice lattes that are back earlier than ever: Believe it or not, holiday collections are already beginning to trickle into stores, including advent calendars.

These aren’t just any blockbuster beauty box sets; advent calendars make the countdown to Christmas the most glam 24 (or, in some cases, 12) days of the year. And there’s one to watch that sells out without fail: Anthropologie.

In recent years, the reader-favorite destination for fashion, home décor, and more has seriously amped up its beauty selection, stocking viral fragrance brands like DedCool and Phlur alongside body-care faves from Salt & Stone, Vacation, and many others. And since 2018, the retailer has compiled some of its bestselling brands into an annual advent calendar — aka a jam-packed value set that’s perfect for gifting, including to yourself.

The 24 Days of Beauty Advent Calendar, $98

And pretty much all of them can be found in the brand’s 24 Days of Beauty Advent Calendar. Retailing for $98 (but with a value of $301), this collection includes full-size and mini goodies from L’Occitane, Caudalie, Boy Smells, Stila, and more, all tucked inside a keepsake box featuring artwork by British-Filipina artist Nephthus Foster, whom Anthropologie has partnered with for the past three years on its holiday designs.

The 12 Days of Beauty Advent Calendar, $50

Looking for a more budget-friendly (but every bit as fun) unboxing experience? There’s also the 12 Days of Beauty Advent Calendar. For $50 (valued at $128), you’ll find minis from OPI, ILIA Beauty, Megababe, and more. (Pro tip: Repurpose the Lovers for Life-designed box to house trinkets like jewelry, love notes, and more.)

And even though it’s barely September, we wouldn’t be surprised to see both calendars sell out by the time the leaves turn — because nothing haunts us quite like the beauty advent calendars we missed out on.

title: Why Adults Is The Buzziest Show On TV, According To Star Lucy Freyer
text:
Why Adults Is The Buzziest Show On TV, According To Star Lucy Freyer

FX’s Adults is one of the buzziest new shows around. It’s a show that embraces the realities of life as a Gen-Zer in this chaotic world, and although it’s a laugh-out-loud comedy, it doesn’t shy away from real-world topics. In Season 1, there was an episode devoted to the cost of healthcare in the US, and the cliffhanger saw Paul Baker (Jack Innanen) struggle to immigrate as a Canadian citizen. Season 2 examines even more real-world issues, including language use, fear of aging as women, and our digital footprint. Lucy Freyer, the Australian star who plays Billie Schaeffer, tells Refinery29 that this could be why Adults resonates with so many viewers. Season 2 spoilers follow.

In Season 1, Issa Damani (Amita Rao) takes in a young teenager, Annabelle, who needs an abortion. Due to reproductive laws, she’s had to travel to New York to receive healthcare. The episode escalates, with Annabelle portrayed as an unlikeable, whiny character — but the point is clear. Everybody should have the right to reproductive healthcare, even if they’re annoying. “All of these ideas are packaged in this way that is sort of fun and easy. But when you think about it, you’re like, oh. [There’s] actually a lot to think about,” Freyer laughs.

In Season 2, Episode 7 “C Alert”, Anton Evans (Owen Thiele) gets in trouble when dropping the word “cunt” (complimentary) in a corporate setting. Many people from the LGBQTIA+ communities have taken back this word and use it in a positive way — see PEDESTRIAN.TV’s “cunty” moment with Pedro Pascal here — but it becomes a whole thing with the older, predominantly white NYC executives.

“When we read it, I was like, ‘Oh, it’s so brilliant!’,” Freyer recalls. “It’s about the evolution of language. David Foster Wallace has this essay that he wrote, which is actually a book review of a dictionary called Authority in American Usage and it’s about language.” She goes on to say that some people allow language to evolve, while others hold on to an idea of the traditional use of language. It’s these types of storylines that make us think deeper and keep us hooked.

One of Billie’s biggest hurdles this season is ageing. It sounds laughable, since her character is only 25, but it’s so easy to feel like you’re fighting an invisible clock. Again, it’s relatable. Freyer says she turned 30 while she was filming that particular episode, and was faced with an actor who played a younger version of her. “She’s so lovely and young, and [I thought], this could spin me out. But you know what? I’m exactly where I need to be, this is great,” Freyer says. “I think now ageing, especially for women, everything is happening later. It doesn’t matter. You don’t have any specific timeline… it used to be this idea of life ends when you turn 30, but [now] it’s like life feels like it’s just beginning, and in a big way.”

Part of the reason Freyer thinks the “ticking clock” conversation isn’t as relevant now is due to health technology advances like egg freezing and IVF — another big storyline in Adults Season 2. “Specifically for women who want to have [biological] children, there is that biological clock that sort of starts to play into the way you think about your existence after you turn 30,” the actor says. “I think now with egg freezing, it’s opened up a world for women to be like, actually, you know what? I’m going to throw those things on ice and live my life the way I want to live it, and not [have it] dictated by that timeline.”

The other big drawcard for Adults is that friendship sits at the heart of every episode. Friends are your chosen family, and seeing what Billie and the gang get up to in each episode can either give you nostalgia for earlier days or something to look forward to. “To be able to live with friends when things sort of don’t matter that much is the greatest joy you can possibly have in life,” Freyer declares. “Especially friendship when proximity is easy.”

The actor notes that when you get older, it becomes harder to have regular, quality time with your friends, even just because of location and schedules. But the sweet spot for Adults is the setting: when you still have housemates and can be so entrenched in each other’s lives. “When you’re living with your friends, and you don’t have things on in your life that matter that much, friendships can be the centre of your life,” she says.

“Issa and Billie’s relationship in this season, the way they explore it and how we end up sharing a room… I think that it’s such a beautiful depiction of friendship in your 20s.”

Adults Season 2 is now available to stream on FX.

title: Gabriella Karefa-Johnson On Owning Her Space, Hidden London Gems & The Rules Of Plane Perfume
text:
Gabriella Karefa-Johnson On Owning Her Space, Hidden London Gems & The Rules Of Plane Perfume

Besides a pilot, you’d be hard-pressed to find someone as well-traveled as Gabriella Karefa-Johnson. From the winding streets of London and the cobblestones of Paris to the glittering sands of Jamaica, the New York-based fashion editor and stylist — who made history as the first Black woman to style the cover of Vogue — has amassed a lifetime of memories, experiences, and, naturally, scents from the destinations that have shaped her work. Getting there, however, hasn’t always been smooth sailing — or flying.

“It’s difficult to exist sometimes in marginalized bodies,” says Karefa-Johnson, “so when you’re in this kind of like, rarefied air — as some might call first class — it can feel alienating, like there are eyes on you, like you’re not supposed to be there.” One thing she’ll never do? Shrink. “Or camouflage,” says Karefa-Johnson. “I’m going to be me wherever I am, and I think that that’s why I feel so comfortable in these places, because I bring myself authentically.”

London — in particular the eclectic melting pot that is Brixton — is one such place where she can truly be herself, with the surrounding scents creating memories that linger long after the vacation ends. But beyond the powdery, soapy blend of cashmeran, musk, and patchouli that makes the iconic Rosewood Hotel’s pillow mist so unforgettable, it’s the city’s everyday food smells that stay with her most: “Think fish and chips all wrapped in a newspaper, so you have that paper smell,” says Karefa-Johnson.

Ultimately, though, nowhere smells as good as home. “I want to be smelling like — honestly and truthfully — my mom,” says Karefa-Johnson. “I haven’t seen my mom in a really long time [but] I want to go back home to hug her more. I want to be around her enough for her brilliance to rub off on me. And I want to prioritize being with my family that is all in LA; I miss them dearly.” So what does that feeling of comfort smell like? EOS Vanilla Cashmere 24H Moisture Body Lotion, Body Wash, and Body Mist, of course.

Listen to the full podcast episode, where Karefa-Johnson joins Nose Dive host Asia Grant — an NYC-based independent perfumer and creative director — for a conversation about taking up space and being unapologetically herself, the best-smelling London hotspots, and the scents she’d avoid wearing on a plane.
